subtype: Approach: uses good enough for low-stakes decisions to save mental energy [Thinking]
passage: I'm Akash, and my room is next to Ritu's on the hostel's second floor. Two weeks before exams the zip on Ritu's laptop bag broke. I expected a long research session, because Ritu compares everything, even biscuits. Instead Ritu said, 'Under eight hundred rupees, padded pocket. That's it.' Ritu looked at two websites, picked the first bag that fit both, ordered it in ten minutes and closed the tab. I asked whether a better one might exist. 'Probably. Not worth an evening,' said Ritu, and opened the physics notes. I can't tell whether Ritu was truly at ease or just forcing it, but the bag arrived on Thursday and the notes got the whole evening.

qa.q: Which two conditions did Ritu set for the bag?
qa.a: Ritu set the conditions of under eight hundred rupees and a padded pocket.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling when saying 'Not worth an evening'?
qa.a: Ritu was probably calm about a small decision, though Akash cannot be sure whether it was real ease or forced.

qa.q: What other approach could Ritu use if unsure about the bag?
qa.a: Ritu could ask a hostel-mate who owns a similar bag how it has held up, which takes a minute and adds a check without a long search.

qa.q: How might Akash have seen Ritu's quick choice?
qa.a: Akash was probably surprised, since Ritu compares everything, and curious about how the choice was made so fast. 🙂

grounding: Shows a hostel student choosing a laptop bag by two criteria and stopping there, saving hours of comparison for exam preparation.

subtype: Approach: sets the bar too low on an important decision [Pitfall]
passage: Mohit, before you sign anything on Saturday, let me tell you about my first flat. I'm Ankita, and at twenty-four I saw one flat, and it had a bed, a working tap and a rent I could afford. I had decided beforehand that it only needed to be 'fine', the way I choose a phone case. So I said yes that evening. I never read the lease properly, and I never travelled the route to work at eight in the morning. My cousin Divya visited in the third month and asked how I survived the trip. It took ninety minutes with two changes, and the lease held my deposit for a year. I stayed, tired, until the year ended. A phone case I could replace; a year I couldn't.

qa.q: How long did the commute take?
qa.a: The commute took ninety minutes with two changes.

qa.q: What did Ankita feel while staying until the year ended?
qa.a: Ankita felt tired and probably regretful, stuck with a choice made too quickly.

qa.q: Which choice caused most of the trouble, and what could have been done differently?
qa.a: Saying yes that evening without reading the lease or travelling the route caused it, and both checks could have been done before signing.

qa.q: How might Divya have seen Ankita's daily trip?
qa.a: Divya was likely worried and surprised by the long trip, which is why Divya asked how Ankita survived it.

grounding: Shows a young professional accepting the first flat that meets basic needs without checking the lease or the commute, a standard that suits a cheap purchase but not a year-long commitment.

subtype: Approach: raises the threshold after noticing the stakes and rechecks options [Revision]
passage: Mohit, you're about to rent your first place, so I'll tell you what I did at your age. I'm Radhika. I had found a flat I liked, and I was ready to say yes, my list ticked: bed, tap, near a bus stop. Then the landlord mentioned that the lease ran eleven months, and something clicked: this wasn't a phone case, it was where I'd wake up every day for a year. I went home and added lines to my list: noise at night, whether water comes all day, and what earlier tenants say about the landlord. The landlord didn't mind my questions and gave me two tenants' numbers. I visited two more flats. One had a wedding hall next door; another had water for only two hours a day. So I took the first one after all, and slept easy.

qa.q: How many months did the lease run?
qa.a: The lease ran eleven months.

qa.q: What was Radhika thinking when 'something clicked'?
qa.a: Radhika realised the flat was a big commitment and not a small purchase, and felt a new seriousness about choosing.

qa.q: Which turning point changed Radhika's approach, and how?
qa.a: Hearing that the lease ran eleven months changed it, since Radhika then added noise, water and the landlord's record to the list and looked at more flats.

qa.q: How did the landlord seem to see Radhika's questions?
qa.a: The landlord didn't mind them and gave two tenants' numbers, which suggests openness to being checked.

grounding: Shows a person realising a rental is a big commitment, adding criteria such as noise, water and the landlord's reputation, and visiting two more flats before deciding.

subtype: Approach: scores options against weighted criteria in a table [Thinking]
passage:
Friday: Ramesh, sixteen, had three streams to choose from after Class 10, and every relative told him something different. Kashish, his cousin, said, 'Put it on paper.' He drew a table with four rows: interest, job outlook, effort, distance of the college.

Saturday: He gave weights out of ten: interest 5, job outlook 3, effort 1, distance 1. Then he scored each stream from one to five on every row. Science scored high on interest and middling on effort.

Sunday: He multiplied and added. Science 42, commerce 35, arts 34. He looked at the numbers for a while and said, 'Okay. Science. But I'll talk it over with Papa tonight.'

qa.q: What weight did Ramesh give to interest?
qa.a: Ramesh gave interest a weight of 5.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's plan to talk with Papa suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: Ramesh is still a little cautious and wants his family's support, even though the numbers favour science.

qa.q: What other approach could Ramesh add to his table?
qa.a: Ramesh could ask students already in each stream what their days are like, since it shows the effort and interest scores from real experience.

qa.q: How might Kashish have seen the table?
qa.a: Kashish probably saw it as a way to calm the noise of relatives' opinions and turn a muddle into something Ramesh can look at.

grounding: Shows a student listing interest, job outlook, effort and college distance after Class 10, weighting them, scoring each stream and comparing totals.

subtype: Approach: builds the matrix in a spreadsheet and adjusts weights to see how the ranking changes [Action]
passage: Sunday night. Three offers, one spreadsheet. Columns: salary, learning, location, growth. I scored each offer 1 to 5 in every column, then set weights. First pass: salary 4, learning 3, location 2, growth 3. Offer B won, mostly on pay. Then I got curious and moved the weights around. Learning up to 5: B and C tie. Location up to 5: C wins clearly. Salary down to 1: C wins again. So C wins in almost every tilt except when salary is everything. Sent the sheet to Disha, who wrote back, 'So why did you start with pay so high?' Fair question. Tomorrow I'll ask myself whether I'm fine earning a bit less at C. — Pallavi

qa.q: Which offer won on the first pass?
qa.a: Offer B won on the first pass, mostly on pay.

qa.q: How does Pallavi feel about the result?
qa.a: Pallavi feels curious and thoughtful, and is still checking whether earning a bit less at C would be acceptable.

qa.q: What other step could Pallavi take before deciding?
qa.a: Pallavi could speak to a current employee at C about daily work, since a matrix cannot show what the days feel like.

qa.q: How might Disha have seen Pallavi's first weighting?
qa.a: Disha probably felt that pay was weighted too heavily, which is why Disha asked why Pallavi started with it so high.

grounding: Shows a student putting three job offers into a spreadsheet and changing the weights to test whether the winning offer holds up.

subtype: Approach: fudges scores to make the matrix confirm a favourite [Pitfall]
passage: Gargi, I have to admit something about the college table I showed you. I'm Jomon, and I built it in a spreadsheet: fees, placements, campus, city. But I had already fallen for the college in Pune the day I saw its campus video. So, without exactly deciding to, I gave Pune 5 for 'campus feel' and 'city', and the others 2 and 3 on the same rows. Placements I scored fairly, because those numbers were public. Pune won by a mile. It looked so tidy that I showed it to my parents as proof. Then you asked, 'What did you base the campus scores on for the other two?' and I realised I had never even visited them. The table wasn't a decision. It was my decision, dressed up.

qa.q: Which college won the table?
qa.a: The college in Pune won the table.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when Gargi asked about the campus scores?
qa.a: Jomon felt exposed and a little ashamed, realising the scores had no basis since the other two had never been visited.

qa.q: What other approach could Jomon use to make the table fair?
qa.a: Jomon could set the scoring rules before naming any college, visit the other two, and let Gargi score the same rows independently.

qa.q: How might Jomon's parents have seen the table?
qa.a: Jomon's parents probably saw solid proof, trusting the tidy numbers, which is why they could be misled about how the choice was made.

grounding: Shows a student who loves one college giving it high subjective scores and rivals low ones, so tidy numbers hide a decision made beforehand.

subtype: Approach: uses the matrix to expose which criterion truly drives a choice [Thinking]
passage: Anirban, you're weighing three flats, so listen to this. I'm Reena. When my friends Kabir and Sana were choosing, they made a table with rent, size, light, safety and commute. They weighted it three different ways: money first, space first, comfort first. Every time, the flat with the shortest commute came out on top. Sana laughed and said, 'It isn't even close, is it? We keep saying we want space, but we hate the road.' Kabir added that they'd spent years arguing over late arrivals. They took the small flat near the metro. What the table gave them wasn't so much an answer as the truth about themselves.

qa.q: In how many different ways did Kabir and Sana weight the table?
qa.a: They weighted it three different ways.

qa.q: What was Sana feeling when laughing and saying 'It isn't even close'?
qa.a: Sana was amused and a little surprised to see that the commute mattered most, more than the space they said they wanted.

qa.q: Which step in the story showed what they truly cared about?
qa.a: Trying three different weightings showed it, since the shortest commute won each time.

qa.q: How might Kabir have felt about the result?
qa.a: Kabir was probably relieved to have the reason clear, since they had spent years arguing over late arrivals.

grounding: Shows a couple comparing flats and noticing that whichever weights they use, commute time decides, revealing what they care about.

subtype: Approach: notices a gut feeling against the top score and revisits the criteria [Revision]
passage: The offer deadline was Friday noon, and it was Thursday at ten at night when Rajni finished the table: pay, title, size of the employer, growth. Company A scored highest by a clear margin. Rajni looked at the number and felt her stomach tighten, the same feeling she got when she pictured Monday mornings there. She called Raghav, a friend, who asked, 'What's missing from your table?' Rajni typed two new rows: team culture, and what the daily work would actually feel like. Her interviews at A had been with cold, hurried people, and the role was mostly reports. She rescored. Company B moved from second place to first. She stared at it for a minute, then sent B her acceptance at nine on Friday.

qa.q: What was the offer deadline?
qa.a: The offer deadline was Friday noon.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel on seeing that Company A scored highest?
qa.a: Rajni felt dread, as her stomach tightened at the thought of Monday mornings there.

qa.q: What other approach could Rajni use to check team culture?
qa.a: Rajni could ask to speak with a future teammate at each company, since a direct chat shows the culture better than an interview panel.

qa.q: How might Raghav have seen Rajni's first table?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt it left out something important, which is why Raghav asked what was missing.

grounding: Shows a person noticing that a matrix favours a job she dreads, asking what is missing, adding team culture and daily work, and seeing the ranking change.

subtype: Approach: solves a new problem by comparing it with a familiar one [Thinking]
passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof, and Reena, five, wanted to open the new jar of jam for her toast. She pulled the lid straight up. Nothing. She pushed it. Nothing. Then she stopped and thought of Amma with the pickle jar: Amma held the jar with one hand and turned the lid round and round. Reena held the jar against her tummy and turned. The lid gave a small squeak, then moved. 'Amma, I did it like the pickle jar!' she shouted over the rain. Amma laughed and handed her a spoon.

qa.q: What did Reena want to open?
qa.a: Reena wanted to open the new jar of jam.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when the lid moved?
qa.a: Reena felt proud and excited, shown by her shout over the rain. 😊

qa.q: What could Reena do if the lid still would not move?
qa.a: Reena could ask Amma to loosen it a little first, and then turn it herself.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt hearing Reena's shout?
qa.a: Amma was probably amused and proud, since Amma laughed and handed her a spoon.

grounding: Shows a child who cannot open a new jar remembering how the pickle jar lid is turned and copying that motion.

subtype: Approach: uses an earlier solved problem as a model for a new one [Action]
passage: At school break, Yash had the class bat and five friends all shouting, 'Me first!' He stood by the wall, thinking. It was like the library. Usha Ma'am had solved that last month by letting children borrow books in roll-number order. 'Same thing,' Yash muttered. He tore a page from his rough notebook, wrote the five names in a column, and numbered them one to five. 'After your turn, you go to the bottom,' he told them. 'Tomorrow we start with whoever is next.' Urmila complained for a moment that she was fifth, then nodded. When the bell rang, Yash pinned the list on the wall under the clock.

qa.q: How many friends wanted a turn with the bat?
qa.a: Five friends wanted a turn.

qa.q: What did Yash think when he remembered the library?
qa.a: Yash thought it was the same kind of problem, so the same kind of answer could work, and he felt confident.

qa.q: What could Yash do if a friend was away on the next day?
qa.a: Yash could skip that friend for the day and keep their place at the top, so nobody loses a turn because of being absent.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt about being fifth?
qa.a: Urmila was probably annoyed for a moment, then accepted it once she saw that everyone waits in the same order.

grounding: Shows a boy using the library's roll-number order as a model to set up a rotating list for cricket turns among five friends.
